title: "Week 7 Practice — Cardiac Foundations I–III"
toc-depth: 2
---

**40 practice questions: 28 multiple-choice (70%) + 12 short-response (30%).** Answers and explanations are collapsed initially. Every assigned lecture-review theme is represented either directly or through a closely aligned concept/application question.

# Part A — Multiple Choice

### Question 1 — Cardiac cells {#w07-mc01}

Most cells in the myocardium are:

- **A.** autorhythmic pacemaker cells
- **B.** force-producing contractile myocytes
- **C.** sensory neurons
- **D.** erythrocytes

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Most cardiac cells are contractile myocytes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A small fraction are specialized autorhythmic/conduction cells; the great majority generate force.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 2 — Intercalated discs {#w07-mc02}

Gap junctions in intercalated discs are important because they:

- **A.** permit electrical current to spread between cardiac cells
- **B.** store Ca2+ like the SR
- **C.** prevent all ion movement
- **D.** synthesize hemoglobin

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Gap junctions electrically couple adjacent myocytes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Low-resistance cell-to-cell current flow helps the myocardium behave as a functional syncytium.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 3 — Cardiac E-C coupling {#w07-mc03}

In ventricular myocytes, Ca2+ entering through L-type channels primarily:

- **A.** triggers additional Ca2+ release from SR
- **B.** directly opens nicotinic ACh receptors
- **C.** closes all K+ channels permanently
- **D.** becomes hemoglobin iron

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Trigger Ca²⁺ evokes Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Cardiac contraction depends on extracellular Ca²⁺ entry as the trigger for much larger SR Ca²⁺ release.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 4 — Relaxation {#w07-mc04}

Which process contributes to lowering cytosolic Ca2+ during cardiac relaxation?

- **A.** SERCA and Na+/Ca2+ exchange
- **B.** opening nicotinic receptors
- **C.** activating rhodopsin
- **D.** platelet aggregation

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

SERCA and membrane extrusion mechanisms remove cytosolic Ca²⁺.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Relaxation requires Ca²⁺ to leave troponin, which occurs only after the cytosolic Ca²⁺ signal declines.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 5 — Blood flow {#w07-mc05}

Which sequence correctly traces blood from the right ventricle back to the left ventricle?

- **A.** aorta → lungs → vena cava → left atrium
- **B.** pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle
- **C.** vena cava → aorta → lungs → left ventricle
- **D.** pulmonary vein → right atrium → aorta

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Pulmonary arteries carry low-oxygen blood away from the right ventricle; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 6 — Valves {#w07-mc06}

Heart valves open and close primarily because of:

- **A.** active contraction of valve tissue
- **B.** pressure differences across the valves
- **C.** electrical stimulation from motor neurons
- **D.** platelet activation

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

Pressure gradients determine valve position.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
When upstream pressure exceeds downstream pressure, a valve is pushed open; reversal closes it.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 7 — Ventricular AP {#w07-mc07}

The plateau of the ventricular action potential is supported mainly by:

- **A.** prolonged Ca2+ entry balanced by K+ currents
- **B.** only fast Na+ influx for several seconds
- **C.** only Cl− influx
- **D.** cessation of all ion movement

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

L-type Ca²⁺ current helps maintain the plateau.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The plateau prolongs depolarization and therefore the refractory period.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 8 — Tetanus prevention {#w07-mc08}

Cardiac muscle normally cannot be tetanized because:

- **A.** it has no actin
- **B.** its action potential and refractory period are very long
- **C.** it lacks Ca2+
- **D.** it has no autonomic innervation

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

The long refractory period overlaps most of the contraction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A second action potential cannot be triggered early enough to summate contractions into tetanus, preserving time for filling.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 9 — Pacemaker {#w07-mc09}

The SA node normally sets heart rate because it:

- **A.** has the slowest spontaneous depolarization
- **B.** reaches threshold spontaneously faster than other pacemakers
- **C.** is the only tissue with K+ channels
- **D.** is in the left ventricle

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

SA nodal cells have the fastest intrinsic pacemaker rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
They depolarize downstream pacemaker tissues before those tissues reach their own thresholds.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 10 — Funny current {#w07-mc10}

Pacemaker “funny” current contributes most directly to:

- **A.** spontaneous diastolic depolarization
- **B.** ventricular plateau only
- **C.** clot formation
- **D.** skeletal muscle tetanus

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

If contributes to the slow pacemaker depolarization.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The unstable membrane potential drifts toward threshold rather than remaining at a fixed resting value.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 11 — Conduction {#w07-mc11}

Which sequence is correct?

- **A.** AV node → SA node → Purkinje fibers
- **B.** SA node → AV node → His/bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
- **C.** Purkinje fibers → atria → SA node
- **D.** ventricles → SA node → AV node

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

SA node initiates; AV node delays; His–Purkinje distributes to ventricles.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
This ordered conduction supports atrial contraction before coordinated ventricular contraction.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 12 — AV delay {#w07-mc12}

The AV nodal delay is physiologically useful because it:

- **A.** allows ventricular filling after atrial activation
- **B.** prevents atrial depolarization entirely
- **C.** causes semilunar valves to remain open
- **D.** stops the SA node

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

It provides time for atria to contract and ventricles to fill before ventricular systole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Without appropriate delay, atrial and ventricular contractions would overlap more and reduce filling efficiency.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 13 — ECG {#w07-mc13}

The P wave represents:

- **A.** atrial depolarization
- **B.** ventricular depolarization
- **C.** ventricular repolarization
- **D.** atrial contraction force

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

P wave = atrial depolarization.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Electrical depolarization precedes the mechanical atrial contraction it initiates.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 14 — ECG {#w07-mc14}

The QRS complex represents:

- **A.** atrial depolarization
- **B.** ventricular depolarization
- **C.** ventricular repolarization
- **D.** AV valve closure only

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

QRS = ventricular depolarization.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Atrial repolarization occurs around the same time but is usually obscured by the much larger ventricular signal.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 15 — ECG {#w07-mc15}

The T wave represents:

- **A.** ventricular repolarization
- **B.** atrial depolarization
- **C.** SA node firing only
- **D.** ventricular filling volume

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

T wave = ventricular repolarization.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The ECG records electrical events, not pressure or volume directly.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 16 — ECG interpretation {#w07-mc16}

An ECG directly measures:

- **A.** surface electrical potential differences generated by cardiac activity
- **B.** ventricular pressure
- **C.** stroke volume
- **D.** valve opening area

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

ECG is an electrical recording.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Mechanical events follow electrical activation but must be inferred or measured by other techniques.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 17 — Cardiac cycle {#w07-mc17}

During isovolumetric ventricular contraction:

- **A.** AV and semilunar valves are both closed
- **B.** all valves are open
- **C.** ventricular volume rises rapidly
- **D.** ventricular pressure falls

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Both valve sets are closed while pressure rises at constant volume.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The phase begins after AV valve closure and ends when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and semilunar valves open.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 18 — Ejection {#w07-mc18}

The aortic valve opens when:

- **A.** left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
- **B.** aortic pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure
- **C.** left atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
- **D.** the P wave begins

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

A positive ventricular-to-aortic pressure gradient opens the valve.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Valve motion follows pressure, so timing can be predicted from pressure curves on the Wiggers diagram.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 19 — Filling {#w07-mc19}

The mitral valve opens when:

- **A.** left ventricular pressure falls below left atrial pressure
- **B.** left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
- **C.** aortic pressure is maximal
- **D.** the QRS begins regardless of pressure

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

The AV valve opens when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
This ends isovolumetric relaxation and begins ventricular filling.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 20 — Stroke volume {#w07-mc20}

If EDV = 130 mL and ESV = 50 mL, stroke volume is:

- **A.** 50 mL
- **B.** 80 mL
- **C.** 130 mL
- **D.** 180 mL

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

SV = EDV − ESV = 80 mL.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Stroke volume is the amount ejected per beat, not the amount remaining after systole.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 21 — Cardiac output {#w07-mc21}

A heart rate of 75 beats/min and SV of 80 mL/beat gives CO closest to:

- **A.** 0.6 L/min
- **B.** 6.0 L/min
- **C.** 60 L/min
- **D.** 155 L/min

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

CO = 75 × 80 mL/min = 6000 mL/min = 6.0 L/min.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Always convert mL to L if the requested unit is L/min.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 22 — Frank-Starling {#w07-mc22}

The Frank–Starling mechanism predicts that, within physiological limits, increased EDV tends to:

- **A.** increase stroke volume
- **B.** stop pacemaker firing
- **C.** decrease ventricular stretch to zero
- **D.** close all valves

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Greater filling/stretch increases contraction force and SV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
This intrinsic mechanism helps match output to venous return.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 23 — Chronotropy {#w07-mc23}

A positive chronotropic effect means:

- **A.** increased heart rate
- **B.** increased contractile force at the same fiber length
- **C.** increased blood viscosity
- **D.** decreased venous return

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Chronotropy refers to heart rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Sympathetic stimulation is positively chronotropic; parasympathetic vagal activity is negatively chronotropic.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 24 — Inotropy {#w07-mc24}

A positive inotropic effect means:

- **A.** increased myocardial contractility
- **B.** reduced heart rate only
- **C.** reduced blood volume
- **D.** increased sensory firing

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

Inotropy refers to contractile strength independent of preload.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Sympathetic β1 signalling increases Ca²⁺ handling and can reduce ESV, thereby raising SV.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 25 — Sympathetic effect {#w07-mc25}

Sympathetic stimulation of ventricular myocytes increases contractility mainly by:

- **A.** increasing intracellular Ca2+ availability
- **B.** blocking all L-type Ca2+ channels
- **C.** removing troponin
- **D.** decreasing SR Ca2+ uptake permanently

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

β1 signalling enhances Ca²⁺ entry and SR cycling.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
More Ca²⁺ available to troponin increases cross-bridge activation and contraction force.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 26 — Heart sounds {#w07-mc26}

The first heart sound (S1) is associated primarily with:

- **A.** AV valve closure
- **B.** semilunar valve opening
- **C.** atrial depolarization
- **D.** aortic recoil only

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

S1 occurs around closure of the AV valves at the start of ventricular systole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The sound arises from vibrations generated by abrupt changes in flow/valve-associated structures, not from valve leaflets simply “slapping.”

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 27 — PV loop {#w07-mc27}

End-systolic volume is the ventricular volume:

- **A.** just before ventricular contraction
- **B.** remaining after ejection
- **C.** entering the atrium per minute
- **D.** at the peak of the P wave only

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**

ESV is the amount remaining in the ventricle after systole/ejection.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
EDV is the maximum filled volume before contraction; SV is the difference between EDV and ESV.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 28 — Integration {#w07-mc28}

If heart rate rises while stroke volume remains unchanged, cardiac output will:

- **A.** rise
- **B.** fall
- **C.** remain identical
- **D.** become zero

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**

CO = HR × SV, so increasing HR raises CO if SV is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
In real physiology very high HR can reduce filling and SV, but the question explicitly holds SV constant.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

# Part B — Short Response

### Question 29 — Cardiac vs skeletal {#w07-sr01}

Compare cardiac contractile cells with skeletal muscle fibers in cell shape, coupling, Ca²⁺ source, and functional consequence.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cardiac cells are branched, electrically coupled by gap junctions, depend on extracellular trigger Ca²⁺ plus SR release, and cannot tetanize; skeletal fibers are long multinucleated cells, individually innervated, and use mechanically coupled SR release.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A high-quality comparison links structure to function: electrical coupling coordinates the heart, and the long cardiac AP prevents tetanus so pumping can alternate with filling.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 30 — Cardiac E-C coupling {#w07-sr02}

Trace excitation–contraction coupling in a ventricular myocyte.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
AP → L-type Ca²⁺ entry → RyR-mediated SR Ca²⁺ release → troponin activation → cross-bridge cycling; relaxation via SERCA and Ca²⁺ extrusion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The extracellular Ca²⁺ influx is a trigger rather than the entire contractile Ca²⁺ supply. This distinguishes cardiac from skeletal E-C coupling.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 31 — Blood flow {#w07-sr03}

Trace one red blood cell from the vena cava through the heart, lungs, and back to the aorta.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Vena cava → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → aorta.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
This sequence tests chambers, valves, and vessels together. Remember arteries/veins are named by direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 32 — Action potential {#w07-sr04}

Explain the major ionic logic of a ventricular action potential and why its duration matters.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fast depolarization, early repolarization, Ca²⁺-supported plateau, K⁺-mediated repolarization; long duration creates long refractory period and prevents tetanus.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The functional reason for the plateau is as important as ion names: the heart must relax between beats to refill.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 33 — Pacemaker {#w07-sr05}

Explain how SA nodal cells spontaneously reach threshold and how autonomic input can alter heart rate.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Unstable pacemaker potential driven by If and changing Ca²⁺/K⁺ currents reaches threshold; sympathetic input steepens pacemaker depolarization, parasympathetic input slows it/hyperpolarizes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Changing the slope and starting voltage of the pacemaker potential changes how quickly threshold is reached, thereby changing beat frequency.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 34 — Conduction {#w07-sr06}

Trace the cardiac conduction pathway and explain the role of AV nodal delay.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
SA node → atria → AV node → His → bundle branches → Purkinje → ventricles; AV delay allows atrial emptying and ventricular filling before ventricular contraction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The conduction system is not merely a list: its timing organizes pump mechanics.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 35 — ECG {#w07-sr07}

Relate P, QRS, and T waves to electrical events and subsequent mechanical events.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
P = atrial depolarization → atrial contraction; QRS = ventricular depolarization → ventricular contraction; T = ventricular repolarization → relaxation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Electrical events precede mechanical events. The ECG therefore helps time the Wiggers diagram but does not directly record pressure or contraction.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 36 — Wiggers {#w07-sr08}

Draw or describe a Wiggers diagram for one left-heart cycle, including ECG, atrial pressure, ventricular pressure, aortic pressure, LV volume, valve events, and heart sounds.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A complete answer aligns P/QRS/T with filling, isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation; shows mitral/aortic opening/closing and S1/S2.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Use pressure crossings to decide valve events. Use volume constancy to identify isovolumetric phases. This is the most reliable way to build the diagram rather than memorizing a picture.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 37 — Pressure-volume {#w07-sr09}

Explain why ventricular volume stays constant during both isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both inlet and outlet valves are closed during each isovolumetric phase, so pressure changes without blood entering or leaving.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The two phases differ in direction of pressure change: rising after AV valve closure versus falling after semilunar valve closure.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 38 — Cardiac output {#w07-sr10}

Define EDV, ESV, SV, HR, and CO and give the two key equations.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
SV = EDV − ESV; CO = HR × SV. EDV is filled volume before systole, ESV volume remaining after ejection.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
These definitions let you reason through any problem involving changes in filling, contractility, or heart rate.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 39 — Frank-Starling {#w07-sr11}

Explain the Frank–Starling relationship and distinguish it from sympathetic inotropy.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Frank–Starling: more filling/preload increases force/SV because of greater fiber stretch; inotropy changes force at a given preload through altered Ca²⁺ handling.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Both can raise SV but by different mechanisms. One is an intrinsic length-dependent property; the other changes contractile state.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::

### Question 40 — Application {#w07-sr12}

Predict the effect of a β1-adrenergic agonist on SA node, ventricular contractility, ESV, SV, and CO.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
HR and contractility increase; stronger ejection tends to lower ESV and increase SV, so CO rises.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The answer should connect receptor-level sympathetic signalling to both chronotropy and inotropy, then propagate those effects through CO = HR × SV.

**Review:** [Week 7 study guide](../study-guides/week07-cardiac.qmd).
:::
